items.title: Rossano Sportiello interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, October 2, 2015 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: I mean Beethoven and Chopin and Bach and so on. ... Like for example Chopin wrote beautiful melodies, you know, the nocturnes and so for example I played the “Nocturne in E flat,” number two... Chopin could improvise a ballad you know, no problem.

ctx.x: Right. It’s pretty profound. Did you have professors or piano teachers — the classical piano teachers, did they make an issue of you being a jazz player at the same time?

I had only one classical piano teacher. From the beginning, I was age 9 until the final graduation at age 22, and he never was difficult that way. He always let me do what I wanted as far as I would practice also the regular stuff. I mean Beethoven and Chopin and Bach and so on. And as a matter of fact I think that he was also interested, mildly interested, in jazz. But somehow the way he was brought up was too far away from the mentality of a jazz pianist improvising. But I think that inside he might have…
Oh. Well I’m glad he had that experience. It sort of opened his ears a little bit.
